strengths: Significance and basic methodology: PMVB offers a simple interface between solution predictors and existing MIP solvers. Grouping predictions into cardinality constraints is practically useful, and solving all four complementary subproblems preserves global optimality independently of prediction accuracy.

Empirical merits: Experiments cover logistic regression and GNN predictors, two commercial solvers, several combinatorial problems, and unit commitment. Table 2 reports 1.11–1.31× speedups for full solving, suggesting useful benefits beyond finding restricted-region primal solutions.

Originality: The risk-pooling interpretation provides an interpretable perspective on prediction-guided local branching. Theorem 3.1 sensibly uses instance-level accuracy moments to accommodate dependence between variable errors, provided its population moment conditions hold.

Presentation, reproducibility, and limitations: The overall workflow is understandable, and the manuscript supplies pseudocode, dataset-generation details, training budgets, hardware information, and a code link. It explicitly acknowledges the strong independence assumption and possible data-free infeasibility. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent from the described public and synthetic benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—central concentration guarantee: Theorem 2.1 is not established under the stated assumptions. Equation (2) bounds marginal prediction error over instances, but Equation (4) treats this as a correctness bound for each fixed instance and prediction-selected index set. The sets U and L themselves depend on the random prediction. A4's independence conditional on a fixed instance does not establish the unconditional independence or conditional accuracy bounds needed for the subsequent Hoeffding argument. Errors can concentrate together on difficult instances despite good marginal accuracy.

Soundness—practical probability guarantees: Theorem 3.1 requires valid population means and a variance upper bound, but the manuscript gives no finite-sample calibration procedure establishing these conditions after selecting the threshold. Experimental values or estimation procedures for sigma are unspecified, particularly in the data-free setting. Remark 3.1 strengthens the constraints by substituting predicted probabilities without establishing the calibration needed to retain coverage. Moreover, delta = 0.8 in Section 5.2 gives only a 20% guarantee for each individual inequality and no positive simultaneous guarantee, so these experiments do not substantiate high-probability preservation.

Soundness—additional proof gaps: Theorem 4.1 bounds the number of variables in U that leave the optimal support, then asserts that the bound for L follows from complementarity. The reverse set difference can have a different cardinality and needs a separate argument. Section 3.2 also incorrectly states that excluding all global optima from the preferred region makes every complementary region infeasible under its incumbent cut; another region must instead contain a better solution. Even if 'contains' was intended, inexpensive LP-based pruning does not follow automatically.

Evaluation—selection and measurement: Section 5.4 retains only 57 of 132 MIPLIB instances after excluding infeasible preferred regions and joint timeouts. This outcome-dependent filtering prevents the reported 16% improvement from establishing performance on the original benchmark population; failures and fallback costs should be included. Section 5.2 measures time to a target selected by PMVB's own 120-second run. This is informative but needs equal-budget solution-quality or primal-integral comparisons to support broader efficiency claims.

Originality and significance are insufficiently isolated: Cardinality branching, local branching, and prediction-guided distance restrictions are already acknowledged in the related work, including references [13], [14], and [23]. Comparisons against stock solvers do not establish the incremental benefit of the probabilistic construction. Direct comparisons and ablations against fixed-radius neighborhoods and prediction-based variable fixing are needed to distinguish the proposed contribution from established mechanisms.

Reproducibility and evidential precision: Solver versions, random seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, and whether timings include prediction and root-LP preprocessing are not adequately specified. SCUC uses only five test instances per configuration. Larger SCP training labels permit a 10% optimality gap, whereas the theory concerns optimal labels, without analyzing this mismatch. Table 4 contains 30 entries, including a duplicated blp-ar98, despite reporting evaluation on 57 instances. These omissions make the aggregate results difficult to reconstruct and assess.
